subject: Mathematics
title: Nikhil's Distance Challenge
hook: Nikhil's bike has a broken speedometer. He knows his speed over time but needs to find total distance traveled. Integration is his answer.

slides.title: Integrals
slides.storyContext: Nikhil's speedometer is broken, but his GPS logs speed v(t) every second. To find distance, he reverses differentiation — that's integration.

slides.title: The Broken Speedometer
slides.storyContext: Nikhil's data: v(t) = 20 − 2t m/s (speed decreasing linearly over time). He knows: distance = integral of speed. Ravi says: integration is the reverse of differentiation. If derivative of position gives velocity, integrating velocity gives position back.

slides.title: What is an Integral?
slides.storyContext: Ravi explains: An integral is the reverse of a derivative. If F'(x) = f(x), then ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C.

points.label: Antiderivative
points.text: F is an antiderivative of f if F'(x) = f(x).

points.label: Indefinite integral
points.text: ∫f(x)dx represents ALL antiderivatives: F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant.

points.label: Constant of integration
points.text: C accounts for the fact that derivative of constant is 0. Different antiderivatives differ by a constant.

example.problem: Find ∫ 3x² dx.
example.solution: We need F(x) such that F'(x) = 3x². F(x) = x³ works because (x³)' = 3x². So ∫ 3x² dx = x³ + C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Integral = reverse of derivative. Antiderivative of f is any function whose derivative is f. Plus C because constants disappear in derivatives.

slides.title: Power Rule and Basic Integration
slides.storyContext: Ravi lists integration rules, starting with the most common.

points.label: Constant multiple
points.text: ∫ k·f(x) dx = k ∫ f(x) dx.

points.label: Sum rule
points.text: ∫ [f(x) + g(x)] dx = ∫ f(x) dx + ∫ g(x) dx.

points.label: Exponential and log
points.text: ∫ e^x dx = e^x + C. ∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C.

example.problem: Find ∫ (5x² + 2x − 3) dx.

slides.inSimpleWords: Power rule: bring exponent down, raise power by 1, divide by new exponent. Same linearity as derivatives.

slides.title: Practice: Integrate Basic Polynomials
slides.storyContext: Nikhil tries his first integrals with Ravi coaching.

example.problem: Find ∫ (4x³ − 6x + 1) dx.
example.solution: ∫ 4x³ dx − ∫ 6x dx + ∫ 1 dx = 4·(x⁴/4) − 6·(x²/2) + x + C = x⁴ − 3x² + x + C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply power rule term by term. Don't forget the constant of integration.

slides.title: Why Integration Matters
slides.storyContext: Nikhil realizes: with Ravi's help, he can now convert speed data into distance. 'My broken speedometer isn't broken anymore!' he shouts.

slides.title: From Velocity to Distance
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma connects physics and math: if v(t) = 20 − 2t, then distance s(t) = ∫ v(t) dt.

points.label: Position from velocity
points.text: s(t) = ∫ v(t) dt. Integrating velocity gives position.

points.label: Finding C
points.text: Use initial condition. If Nikhil starts at s(0) = 0, then C = 0. So s(t) = 20t − t².

example.problem: Nikhil's speed v(t) = 20 − 2t m/s. He starts at position 0. Find position at t = 5 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Integrate velocity to get position. Use initial position to find the constant C.

slides.title: Speed Over Time
slides.storyContext: Nikhil plots his speed on a graph: a downward slope as his legs tire. Ravi points: 'The area under this curve is your distance!'

slides.title: Definite Integral and Area
slides.storyContext: Ravi introduces definite integrals: ∫ᵃᵇ f(x) dx gives the signed area under the curve from x=a to x=b.

points.label: Notation
points.text: ∫ᵃᵇ f(x) dx is the definite integral from a to b (limits of integration).

points.label: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
points.text: ∫ᵃᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is an antiderivative of f.

points.label: Geometric interpretation
points.text: If f(x) ≥ 0, the definite integral equals the area under the curve.

example.problem: Find ∫₀⁵ (20 − 2t) dt (distance traveled from t=0 to t=5).
example.solution: Antiderivative: F(t) = 20t − t². ∫₀⁵ (20−2t) dt = F(5) − F(0) = (100−25) − 0 = 75 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Definite integral has limits (a to b). Fundamental Theorem: evaluate antiderivative at b, subtract at a.

slides.title: Practice: Calculate Distance
slides.storyContext: Nikhil calculates distances on different route segments.

example.problem: Speed v(t) = 15 − t m/s from t = 2 to t = 8. Find distance.

slides.inSimpleWords: Definite integrals measure accumulated quantities over an interval.

slides.title: New Techniques Ahead
slides.storyContext: Ravi shows Nikhil a more complex function on the board: v(t) = 30·e^{−0.1t}. 'For this, we need new techniques,' Ravi says mysteriously.

slides.title: Substitution Method (u-substitution)
slides.storyContext: Some integrals look complex. Ravi teaches substitution to simplify.

points.label: Idea
points.text: Let u = g(x). Then du = g'(x)dx. Rewrite integral in terms of u, integrate, substitute back.

points.label: Example
points.text: ∫ (2x)·cos(x²) dx. Let u = x², du = 2x dx. Then ∫ cos(u) du = sin(u) + C = sin(x²) + C.

example.problem: Find ∫ 3x² · sin(x³) dx.
example.solution: Let u = x³, du = 3x² dx. ∫ sin(u) du = −cos(u) + C = −cos(x³) + C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Substitution simplifies complex integrals. Replace inner function with u, find du, integrate, substitute back.

slides.title: Curved Functions
slides.storyContext: Ravi presents trickier speed functions: v(t) = e^t (exponential acceleration), v(t) = sin(t) (oscillating). 'These need substitution,' he says.

slides.title: Practice: Substitution
slides.storyContext: Nikhil tackles substitution problems.

example.problem: Find ∫ 2x · e^{x²} dx.
example.solution: Let u = x², du = 2x dx. ∫ e^u du = e^u + C = e^{x²} + C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Choose u to be the 'inner' function. Make sure du matches what's left.

slides.title: Area Between Two Curves
slides.storyContext: Nikhil rides alongside his friend. Both their speeds vary over time. What's the total distance difference after 10 seconds?

points.label: Formula
points.text: Area between curves f(x) and g(x) (f ≥ g) from a to b: ∫ᵃᵇ [f(x) − g(x)] dx.

example.problem: Nikhil: v₁(t) = 20−2t. Friend: v₂(t) = 15−t. Find distance difference from t=0 to t=5 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Area between curves = definite integral of (upper curve − lower curve). Shows accumulated difference.

slides.title: Practice: Comparing Two Routes
slides.storyContext: Nikhil plans two cycling routes and compares them.

example.problem: Route A: v(t) = 12 m/s (constant). Route B: v(t) = 10 + t m/s. Find total distance difference from t = 0 to t = 4.
example.solution: ∫₀⁴ [(10 + t) − 12] dt = ∫₀⁴ (t − 2) dt = [t²/2 − 2t]₀⁴ = (8 − 8) − 0 = 0 meters. Same total distance!

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare accumulated quantities by integrating the difference.

slides.title: A Powerful New Tool
slides.storyContext: Nikhil sees another chapter in Ravi's calculus book: 'Integration by Parts.' Ravi grins. 'This one's for products of functions.'

slides.title: Integration by Parts
slides.storyContext: For products of functions, Ravi teaches a powerful technique: integration by parts, based on the product rule for derivatives.

points.label: Formula
points.text: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du

points.label: How to choose
points.text: Let u = function that simplifies on differentiation (logs, polynomials). Let dv = rest.

example.problem: Find ∫ x · e^x dx. Let u = x, dv = e^x dx. Then du = dx, v = e^x. By parts: ∫ x·e^x dx = x·e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x·e^x − e^x + C = e^x(x − 1) + C.
example.solution: ∫ x·e^x dx = e^x(x − 1) + C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Integration by parts reverses the product rule. Choose u and dv so the resulting integral is simpler.

slides.title: Practice: Integration by Parts
slides.storyContext: Nikhil applies integration by parts to a product.

example.problem: Find ∫ x · cos(x) dx. Let u = x, dv = cos(x) dx. Then du = dx, v = sin(x). ∫ x·cos(x) dx = x·sin(x) − ∫ sin(x) dx = x·sin(x) + cos(x) + C.
example.solution: ∫ x·cos(x) dx = x·sin(x) + cos(x) + C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Identify which part differentiates to simplify (u), and which you can easily integrate (dv).

slides.title: Trigonometric Integrals
slides.storyContext: Ravi shows Nikhil that cyclic motions (like a pendulum) also integrate nicely.

points.label: Basic trigonometric integrals
points.text: ∫ sin(x) dx = −cos(x) + C, ∫ cos(x) dx = sin(x) + C, ∫ sec²(x) dx = tan(x) + C

example.problem: Find ∫ 5·cos(2x) dx.
example.solution: ∫ 5·cos(2x) dx. Let u = 2x, du = 2dx, so dx = du/2. ∫ 5·cos(u) · (du/2) = (5/2)·sin(u) + C = (5/2)·sin(2x) + C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sines integrate to cosines (with sign), cosines to sines. Use substitution when the angle is scaled.

slides.title: Challenge: Complex Integration
slides.storyContext: Nikhil's actual speed is v(t) = 30·e^{−0.1t} m/s (exponential decay as he tires). Total distance after 10 seconds?

example.problem: Find s = ∫₀¹⁰ 30·e^{−0.1t} dt.

slides.inSimpleWords: For exponential integrals, use substitution or recall ∫ e^{ax} dx = (1/a)·e^{ax} + C.

slides.title: Numerical Integration
slides.storyContext: Ravi explains: 'Not all integrals have closed-form solutions. Sometimes we approximate numerically.'

points.label: Trapezoidal rule
points.text: Approximate ∫[a to b] f(x) dx ≈ (b-a)/2n · [f(x₀) + 2f(x₁) + 2f(x₂) + ... + f(xₙ)]

points.label: Simpson's rule
points.text: More accurate: use parabolas instead of trapezoids. ∫[a to b] f(x) dx ≈ (b-a)/(3n) · [f(x₀) + 4f(x₁) + 2f(x₂) + 4f(x₃) + ...]

example.problem: Approximate ∫₀¹ e^x dx using trapezoidal rule with n=2. Δx = 0.5. Points: x₀=0, x₁=0.5, x₂=1. f(0)≈1, f(0.5)≈1.649, f(1)≈2.718. Approximation: 0.5/2 · [1 + 2(1.649) + 2.718] ≈ 0.25 · 7.016 ≈ 1.754. (Exact value ≈ 1.718.)
example.solution: Trapezoidal approximation ≈ 1.754, with error ≈ 0.036.

slides.inSimpleWords: Numerical methods approximate integrals when exact answers are hard to compute analytically.

slides.title: The Triumphant Calculation
slides.storyContext: Nikhil finishes his calculation and shows Ravi the result. His GPS data is now transformed into a precise distance—189.6 meters. Ravi nods: 'Now you understand integration: from rate to quantity, from speed to distance.'

slides.title: Improper Integrals
slides.storyContext: Ravi mentions: 'What if the interval is infinite, or the function becomes very large? These are improper integrals.'

points.label: Infinite bounds
points.text: ∫[a to ∞] f(x) dx = lim[b→∞] ∫[a to b] f(x) dx

points.label: Convergence
points.text: An improper integral converges if the limit exists and is finite. Otherwise it diverges.

example.problem: Evaluate ∫[1 to ∞] 1/x² dx.
example.solution: ∫[1 to ∞] 1/x² dx = lim[b→∞] ∫[1 to b] x^(-2) dx = lim[b→∞] [-1/x][1 to b] = lim[b→∞] (-1/b + 1) = 1. The integral converges to 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Improper integrals extend the notion to infinite intervals. Check if they converge or diverge.

slides.title: Practice: Improper Integrals
slides.storyContext: Nikhil tests his understanding with an infinite interval problem.

example.problem: Evaluate ∫[0 to ∞] e^(-x) dx.
example.solution: ∫[0 to ∞] e^(-x) dx = lim[b→∞] [-e^(-x)][0 to b] = lim[b→∞] (-e^(-b) + 1) = 1. The integral converges to 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: For exponential decay, improper integrals over infinite intervals often converge to finite values.

slides.title: What Nikhil Learned
slides.storyContext: Integration reversed differentiation, turning speed data into distance — a practical superpower.

points.text: Integral = reverse of derivative. Antiderivative F satisfies F'(x) = f(x).
Indefinite integral: ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C (C = constant of integration).
Power rule: ∫ x^n dx = x^{n+1}/(n+1) + C.
Definite integral: ∫ᵃᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus).
Substitution and integration by parts simplify complex integrals.
Applications: distance from velocity, area under curves, area between curves, work, volume.

slides.inSimpleWords: Integration finds totals: distance from speed, area from height, accumulation from rate. Core tool for physics and engineering.

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Harvest: Finding Area, Volume, and Balance
hook: A farmer's daughter learns calculus by measuring fields and grain stores

slides.title: Application of Integrals
slides.storyContext: Priya returns to her village for summer break and discovers that calculus isn't abstract—it's alive in the fields, granaries, and river embankments all around her.

image.alt: Application of Integrals — Application of Integrals

slides.title: The Village Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya's father Babuji wants to know the exact area of an irregularly shaped wheat field bounded by the river's curve y = 6x - x² and the irrigation channel y = 0. The government surveyor Ravi says he'll charge 5,000 rupees. Priya says, 'Babuji, I can find it using integrals!' Her father laughs—but she's serious. When she gets the answer in minutes, Babuji realizes his daughter has learned something powerful.

slides.title: Area Between Two Curves
slides.storyContext: Priya draws the boundary curves in the dust. The field is trapped between the parabola y = 6x - x² (the river's curve, opening downward) and the x-axis (the irrigation channel). To find area, she integrates.

points.label: Definition
points.text: The area A between curves y = f(x) and y = g(x) from x = a to x = b (where f(x) ≥ g(x)) is: A = ∫[a to b] (f(x) - g(x)) dx

points.label: Finding limits
points.text: First find where the curves intersect by solving f(x) = g(x). These are the bounds of integration.

points.label: Orientation
points.text: Always integrate (upper curve) − (lower curve). If uncertain, sketch or evaluate at a test point.

example.problem: Priya's field: find area between y = 6x - x² and y = 0. Step 1: Find intersections. 6x - x² = 0 → x(6 - x) = 0 → x = 0 or x = 6. Step 2: Set up integral. A = ∫[0 to 6] (6x - x² - 0) dx = ∫[0 to 6] (6x - x²) dx. Step 3: Integrate. ∫(6x - x²) dx = 3x² - x³/3 + C. Step 4: Evaluate. A = [3(6)² - (6)³/3] − [0] = [108 - 72] = 36 square units.
example.solution: Area = 36 square units. When surveyor Ravi measures it later, he gets the same answer. Priya's father is amazed—no fee charged!

slides.inSimpleWords: To find the area of a region trapped between two curves, subtract the lower curve from the upper curve, then integrate.

slides.title: Practice: Find Field Area
slides.storyContext: Priya's uncle has a field bounded by y = x and y = x².

example.problem: Find area between y = x and y = x² from their intersections. Intersections: x = x² → x(1 - x) = 0 → x = 0 or x = 1. Upper curve: y = x (since x > x² for 0 < x < 1). A = ∫₀¹ (x - x²) dx = [x²/2 - x³/3]₀¹ = (1/2 - 1/3) = 1/6 square units.
example.solution: Area = 1/6 square units. The field is small but perfectly calculus-shaped!

slides.inSimpleWords: Always sketch or find intersections first to identify bounds and the upper/lower curves.

slides.title: Watching the Potter
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother asks her to estimate how much grain can fit in the large earthen pot in the store. Priya watches the potter spin clay on a wheel, creating a curved surface of revolution. 'That's calculus in action!' she realizes.

slides.title: Volume of Solids of Revolution
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother asks her to estimate how much grain can fit in the large earthen pot in the store. The pot is shaped like a solid of revolution—the potter rotated a curve around a vertical axis to form it. Priya realizes: this is calculus!

points.label: Disk Method
points.text: When curve y = f(x) is rotated about the x-axis, volume V = π ∫[a to b] [f(x)]² dx. Each thin slice is a disk with radius f(x).

points.label: Washer Method
points.text: When region between two curves is rotated, V = π ∫[a to b] ([R(x)]² − [r(x)]²) dx, where R = outer radius, r = inner radius.

points.label: Shell Method
points.text: Alternatively, rotate about y-axis using shells: V = 2π ∫[a to b] x · f(x) dx.

example.problem: The potter shapes a pot by rotating y = √x (from x = 0 to x = 4) about the x-axis. Find volume. Using disk method: V = π ∫[0 to 4] (√x)² dx = π ∫[0 to 4] x dx = π [x²/2][0 to 4] = π (8 − 0) = 8π cubic units.
example.solution: Volume = 8π ≈ 25.13 cubic units. Priya tells her mother, 'This pot holds about 25 liters of grain!'

slides.inSimpleWords: Rotate a curve around an axis and use integrals to find the volume of the solid created.

slides.title: Practice: Disk Method
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates volume for a simpler pot shape.

example.problem: Rotate y = 2√x from x = 0 to x = 1 about the x-axis. V = π ∫₀¹ (2√x)² dx = π ∫₀¹ 4x dx = π [2x²]₀¹ = 2π cubic units.
example.solution: Volume = 2π ≈ 6.28 cubic units.

slides.inSimpleWords: Remember to square the radius before integrating. Disk volume = π r² h where h is the thickness.

slides.title: Washer Method for Hollow Solids
slides.storyContext: Some pots have a hollow interior—like a vessel. Priya learns to use the washer method.

points.label: When to use
points.text: When a region between two curves is rotated, creating a solid with a hole.

points.label: Formula
points.text: V = π ∫[a to b] ([R(x)]² − [r(x)]²) dx, where R is outer radius and r is inner radius.

example.problem: Rotate region between y = 2 and y = √x from x = 0 to x = 4 about x-axis. Outer radius R = 2, inner radius r = √x. V = π ∫₀⁴ (4 − x) dx = π [4x − x²/2]₀⁴ = π(16 − 8) = 8π.
example.solution: Volume = 8π ≈ 25.13 cubic units.

slides.inSimpleWords: For hollow shapes, subtract the inner radius squared from the outer radius squared before integrating.

slides.title: Practice: Washer Method
slides.storyContext: Priya models a hollow cylindrical vessel.

example.problem: Rotate region between y = 1 and y = 0.5 from x = 0 to x = 3 about x-axis. V = π ∫₀³ (1 − 0.25) dx = π ∫₀³ 0.75 dx = 0.75π · 3 = 2.25π.
example.solution: Volume = 2.25π ≈ 7.07 cubic units.

slides.inSimpleWords: Washer = disk with hole. Subtract inner area from outer area at each cross-section.

slides.title: A Question from the Surveyor
slides.storyContext: Ravi the surveyor visits Babuji's farm and asks Priya, 'Can you measure the length of that river curve that borders your field? I need it for a water-maintenance project.'

slides.title: Arc Length
slides.storyContext: Ravi the surveyor needs to measure the length of the river's curve that borders Priya's field—for a water-maintenance project. He can't just pace it out. Priya says, 'Use arc length integration!'

points.label: Arc Length Formula
points.text: For smooth curve y = f(x) from x = a to x = b, arc length L = ∫[a to b] √(1 + [f'(x)]²) dx

points.label: Parametric form
points.text: If curve is x = x(t), y = y(t), then L = ∫[α to β] √([dx/dt]² + [dy/dt]²) dt

example.problem: Find arc length of y = 6x - x² from x = 0 to x = 6 (Priya's field boundary). Step 1: Compute derivative. dy/dx = 6 - 2x. Step 2: Set up integral. L = ∫[0 to 6] √(1 + (6 - 2x)²) dx = ∫[0 to 6] √(1 + 36 - 24x + 4x²) dx = ∫[0 to 6] √(4x² - 24x + 37) dx. Step 3: This integral is complex (complete the square, use substitution). After integration, L ≈ 10.7 units.
example.solution: The river's curve is approximately 10.7 units long. Ravi uses this to plan maintenance work.

slides.inSimpleWords: To measure the true length of a curved path, integrate the rate of change in both x and y directions.

slides.title: Practice: Simple Arc Length
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates the arc length of a straight-line segment for practice.

example.problem: Find arc length of y = 2x from x = 0 to x = 3. dy/dx = 2. L = ∫₀³ √(1 + 4) dx = ∫₀³ √5 dx = 3√5 ≈ 6.71 units.
example.solution: Arc length = 3√5. (This should match the straight-line distance formula: √[(3−0)² + (6−0)²] = √45 = 3√5. ✓)

slides.inSimpleWords: For linear functions, arc length should match the Pythagorean distance—a good sanity check.

slides.title: Surface Area of Revolution
slides.storyContext: A metalsmith in the village wants to make decorative water vessels by rotating metal bands into smooth surfaces. Priya helps calculate how much metal is needed—by finding surface area.

points.label: Surface Area Formula (about x-axis)
points.text: S = 2π ∫[a to b] f(x) · √(1 + [f'(x)]²) dx

points.label: Surface Area Formula (about y-axis)
points.text: S = 2π ∫[a to b] x · √(1 + [f'(x)]²) dx

example.problem: Rotate y = √x (x ∈ [0, 4]) about x-axis. Surface area: S = 2π ∫[0 to 4] √x · √(1 + 1/(4x)) dx = 2π ∫[0 to 4] √x · √((4x + 1)/(4x)) dx. After simplification and integration, S ≈ 30.8 square units.
example.solution: The metalsmith needs enough material to cover approximately 30.8 square units of surface.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you rotate a curve around an axis, the surface it sweeps has area = circumference at each point × arc length element.

slides.title: The Metalsmith's Challenge
slides.storyContext: The metalsmith listens as Priya explains surface area of revolution. He nods slowly. 'So you're telling me calculus tells me exactly how much metal I need?' Priya smiles. 'Exactly.'

slides.title: Full Problem: The Grain Silo
slides.storyContext: Babuji plans to build a silo for storing grain. It's shaped like a cone with height 8 m and base radius 3 m, formed by rotating the line y = (3/8)x about the y-axis for 0 ≤ y ≤ 8. Find total volume.

example.problem: A cone is formed by rotating y-values from 0 to 8; at height y, the radius is (3/8) × 8 = 3 at the base, scaling linearly. Using disk method (integrating perpendicular to axis of rotation): at height y, radius r(y) = (3y)/8. Volume = π ∫[0 to 8] [(3y)/8]² dy = π ∫[0 to 8] (9y²/64) dy = (9π/64) × [y³/3][0 to 8] = (9π/64) × (512/3) = (9π × 512)/(64 × 3) = 24π cubic meters.
example.solution: Volume = 24π ≈ 75.4 cubic meters. Babuji can store roughly 75 cubic meters of grain—enough for the monsoon!

slides.inSimpleWords: Real silo volumes are found using calculus, not guesswork.

slides.title: Test Yourself: The River Bridge
slides.storyContext: A new bridge arches over the river, shaped like y = 4 - x² (for -2 ≤ x ≤ 2, measured in meters from the center). Find (a) the area under the arch (cross-sectional area if water fills under it), and (b) the arc length of the arch itself.

points.text: (a) Integrate to find area between y = 4 - x² and y = 0.
(b) Use dy/dx = -2x to set up and evaluate arc length integral.

example.problem: (a) Area = ∫[-2 to 2] (4 - x²) dx = [4x - x³/3][-2 to 2] = (8 - 8/3) − (−8 + 8/3) = (16/3) − (−16/3) = 32/3 ≈ 10.67 m². (b) Arc length = ∫[-2 to 2] √(1 + 4x²) dx ≈ 9.29 m (use numerical methods or table of integrals).
example.solution: Area ≈ 10.67 m²; Arc length ≈ 9.29 m. Engineers use these to plan reinforcement.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply area and arc length formulas to a real-world bridge design.

slides.title: Balance in All Things
slides.storyContext: Babuji wonders: where should he position a support beam under his granary door to balance it perfectly? Priya smiles. 'That's the centroid—another integral application!'

slides.title: Centroid and Center of Mass
slides.storyContext: Babuji wonders where to position a support beam under his granary door to balance it perfectly. Priya explains: this is the centroid of the region.

points.label: Centroid x-coordinate
points.text: x̄ = (1/A) ∫[a to b] x·f(x) dx, where A is the area.

points.label: Centroid y-coordinate
points.text: ȳ = (1/A) ∫[a to b] (1/2)[f(x)]² dx (for region under y = f(x)).

example.problem: Find centroid of region under y = 6x - x² from x = 0 to x = 6. Area A = 36 (from earlier). x̄ = (1/36) ∫₀⁶ x(6x - x²) dx = (1/36) ∫₀⁶ (6x² - x³) dx = (1/36)[2x³ - x⁴/4]₀⁶ = (1/36)[432 - 324] = (1/36)·108 = 3. ȳ = (1/36) ∫₀⁶ (1/2)(6x - x²)² dx. After simplification, ȳ ≈ 2.4. Centroid is at (3, 2.4).
example.solution: The centroid is at (3, 2.4). This is where Babuji should place the support to balance the granary load.

slides.inSimpleWords: The centroid is the center of mass—the balance point of a 2D region.

slides.title: Practice: Finding Centroids
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates the centroid of a simpler region.

example.problem: Find centroid of region under y = x from x = 0 to x = 2. Area A = ∫₀² x dx = [x²/2]₀² = 2. x̄ = (1/2) ∫₀² x·x dx = (1/2) ∫₀² x² dx = (1/2)[x³/3]₀² = (1/2)·(8/3) = 4/3. ȳ = (1/2) ∫₀² (1/2)x² dx = (1/4) ∫₀² x² dx = (1/4)·(8/3) = 2/3. Centroid is at (4/3, 2/3).
example.solution: Centroid at (4/3, 2/3). This is the 'center' of the triangular region.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use weighted averages of x and y coordinates to find the balance point of a region.

slides.title: Shell Method for Volume
slides.storyContext: An alternative to disk/washer methods: the shell method. Useful when rotating about y-axis.

points.label: Formula
points.text: When rotating about y-axis: V = 2π ∫[a to b] x · f(x) dx. Picture cylindrical shells.

points.label: When to use
points.text: Use when rotating about y-axis and x is the natural variable.

example.problem: Rotate y = x from x = 0 to x = 2 about y-axis. V = 2π ∫₀² x · x dx = 2π ∫₀² x² dx = 2π [x³/3]₀² = 2π · (8/3) = 16π/3.
example.solution: Volume = 16π/3 ≈ 16.76 cubic units.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shell method: rotate about y-axis, integrate x · height × circumference.

slides.title: Practice: Shell Method
slides.storyContext: Priya applies the shell method to a pottery bowl.

example.problem: Rotate y = √x from x = 0 to x = 4 about y-axis. V = 2π ∫₀⁴ x · √x dx = 2π ∫₀⁴ x^(3/2) dx = 2π [2x^(5/2)/5]₀⁴ = 2π · (2·32/5) = 128π/5.
example.solution: Volume = 128π/5 ≈ 80.42 cubic units.

slides.inSimpleWords: With the shell method, you often integrate powers and roots more easily than with disk/washer.

slides.title: Engineering Precision
slides.storyContext: Priya realizes: calculus gives her engineering precision without costly measurement mistakes. She's become an invaluable helper to her father.

slides.title: Work and Force: Another Application
slides.storyContext: Work = force × distance. But when force varies, integration is needed.

points.label: Variable force
points.text: Work W = ∫[a to b] F(x) dx, where F(x) is force as a function of position.

points.label: Spring force
points.text: For a spring: F(x) = kx. Work to stretch from 0 to d: W = ∫₀ᵈ kx dx = (1/2)kd².

example.problem: Spring constant k = 100 N/m. Work to stretch 0.5 m: W = ∫₀^0.5 100x dx = 100[x²/2]₀^0.5 = 50 · 0.25 = 12.5 J.
example.solution: Work = 12.5 joules.

slides.inSimpleWords: When force changes with position, integrate force over distance to find work.

slides.title: Practice: Calculating Work
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates work for pumping water from a tank.

example.problem: Pump water from a tank 2 m tall. Weight of water at depth x: w(x) = 100(2-x) N. Work to pump out all water: W = ∫₀² 100(2-x) dx = 100[2x - x²/2]₀² = 100(4 - 2) = 200 J.
example.solution: Work = 200 joules.

slides.inSimpleWords: Work integrals combine force and distance. Set up carefully: identify what varies and over what range.

slides.title: Moments and Inertia
slides.storyContext: Priya's physics textbook mentions moment of inertia—another integral application. 'Everything connects,' she muses.

slides.title: Moment of Inertia
slides.storyContext: Rotational motion requires moment of inertia, which measures how mass is distributed around an axis.

points.label: Definition
points.text: I = ∫ r² dm, where r is distance from the axis and dm is a mass element.

points.label: For a 1D rod
points.text: I = ∫[a to b] x² ρ(x) dx, where ρ(x) is linear mass density.

example.problem: Uniform rod of length L and mass M, rotating about one end. Linear density: ρ = M/L. I = ∫₀ᴸ x² (M/L) dx = (M/L) [x³/3]₀ᴸ = (M/L) · (L³/3) = ML²/3.
example.solution: Moment of inertia I = ML²/3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Moment of inertia is the rotational equivalent of mass. It determines how easily an object spins.

slides.title: Practice: Moment of Inertia
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates inertia for a disk.

example.problem: Uniform disk of radius R and mass M, rotating about its center. I = ∫₀ᴿ r² · (2πrρ) dr, where ρ = M/(πR²) is surface density. I = 2πρ ∫₀ᴿ r³ dr = 2πρ [r⁴/4]₀ᴿ = (2π · M/(πR²)) · (R⁴/4) = MR²/2.
example.solution: Moment of inertia I = MR²/2.

slides.inSimpleWords: For symmetric shapes, moment of inertia depends on the shape and axis. Formulas often have nice simple forms.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Area between curves: integrate (upper − lower) over the region.
Volume by revolution: use disk, washer, or shell methods depending on axis and region.
Arc length: ∫√(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx measures true path length.
Surface area of revolution: 2π × radius × arc element.
Centroid: the balance point of a region, found by averaging x and y over the area.
Shell method: alternative for rotation about y-axis using 2π ∫ x · f(x) dx.
Work integrals: apply when force varies with distance or position.
Always sketch the region, identify bounds, and choose the right method.
Real applications: crop fields, storage vessels, bridge designs, water infrastructure, balance, work.

slides.inSimpleWords: Integrals measure areas, volumes, lengths, surface areas, balance points, and work done—the foundation of engineering.

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Medicine: How Things Change Over Time
hook: A pharmacist's son learns how differential equations predict medicine levels in the blood

slides.title: Differential Equations
slides.storyContext: Arjun notices that when his father dispenses medicine, doctors always ask: 'How fast does it leave the body?' This rate of change is governed by differential equations—the heartbeat of physics, biology, and engineering.

slides.title: The Medication Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun's younger sister takes an antibiotic. The dosage is 250 mg at noon. By evening, the nurse measures the drug concentration in her blood: 200 mg. By next morning: 160 mg. Arjun asks his father, 'Is she getting worse?' Dr. Meena smiles. 'No—the body eliminates a fixed fraction of drug every few hours. If we know this rate, we can predict concentration at any time.' Arjun thinks: 'That sounds like a differential equation!' He's right.

slides.title: What is a Differential Equation?
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi, Arjun's teacher, draws an equation on the board involving a function y and its derivative dy/dx. 'This is a differential equation—it says how y changes as x changes.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A differential equation is an equation relating a function y and its derivatives dy/dx, d²y/dx², etc.

points.label: Order
points.text: The order is the highest derivative present. dy/dx + 2y = 0 is first-order. d²y/dx² - 5dy/dx + 6y = 0 is second-order.

points.label: Solution
points.text: A solution is a function y(x) that satisfies the equation when substituted back.

points.label: General vs Particular
points.text: General solution has arbitrary constants (C₁, C₂, ...). Particular solution results from initial conditions (y at a specific x).

example.problem: Consider dy/dx = 3x². Find the general solution. Integrate: y = ∫3x² dx = x³ + C. Verify: dy/dx = d(x³ + C)/dx = 3x². ✓
example.solution: General solution is y = x³ + C. If y(0) = 5 (initial condition), then 5 = 0 + C, so C = 5 and particular solution is y = x³ + 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: A differential equation relates a quantity and how fast it changes. The solution is the quantity as a function.

image.alt: What is a Differential Equation? — Differential Equations

slides.title: Practice: Verify a Solution
slides.storyContext: Arjun verifies that a candidate function solves a differential equation.

example.problem: Verify that y = e^{2x} is a solution to dy/dx = 2y. dy/dx = d(e^{2x})/dx = 2e^{2x}. And 2y = 2e^{2x}. They match! ✓
example.solution: y = e^{2x} is indeed a solution to dy/dx = 2y.

slides.inSimpleWords: To verify a solution, differentiate it and check that it satisfies the original equation.

slides.title: The Pattern Emerges
slides.storyContext: Arjun studies his sister's medication data. He notices: each day, the amount becomes about 80% of the previous day. 'That's exponential!' he realizes. 'And it matches a differential equation.'

slides.title: Separable Differential Equations
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi teaches: 'Some equations are easy to solve if we can separate variables.' Arjun sees this as the key to the medicine problem.

points.label: Form
points.text: An equation of the form dy/dx = f(x) · g(y) is separable if we can rearrange as dy/g(y) = f(x) dx.

points.label: Method
points.text: Integrate both sides: ∫(1/g(y)) dy = ∫f(x) dx + C.

points.label: Exponential decay
points.text: Common in nature: dM/dt = -kM (medicine leaving body). Solution: M(t) = M₀ e^(-kt), where M₀ is initial amount.

example.problem: Model Arjun's sister's medicine: dM/dt = -0.1M, where M is drug amount in mg and t is time in hours. Initial dose M(0) = 250 mg. Separate: dM/M = -0.1 dt. Integrate: ln|M| = -0.1t + C. At t=0: ln(250) = C. So ln(M) = -0.1t + ln(250). Solve: M(t) = 250 e^(-0.1t). At t=8 (evening): M(8) = 250 e^(-0.8) ≈ 250 × 0.449 ≈ 112 mg. At t=24 (next morning): M(24) = 250 e^(-2.4) ≈ 250 × 0.091 ≈ 23 mg.
example.solution: M(t) = 250 e^(-0.1t). The concentration decays exponentially. After 24 hours, only ~23 mg remains, so a second dose is needed.

slides.inSimpleWords: If a rate of change is proportional to the quantity (dy/dx = ky), the solution is exponential growth or decay.

slides.title: Practice: Solve Exponential Decay
slides.storyContext: Arjun solves a similar DE with different numbers.

example.problem: Solve dP/dt = -0.05P with P(0) = 1000. Separate and integrate: ln|P| = -0.05t + C. At t=0: C = ln(1000). P(t) = 1000 e^(-0.05t). At t = 20: P(20) = 1000 e^(-1) ≈ 368 units.
example.solution: P(t) = 1000 e^(-0.05t). After 20 time units, about 37% remains.

slides.inSimpleWords: Separable DEs with dP/dt = kP always solve to P(t) = P₀ e^(kt). If k < 0, decay; if k > 0, growth.

slides.title: Adding Input to Decay
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi presents a new scenario: 'What if the medicine continues to enter the body while it's leaving? Now you need a more powerful technique.'

slides.title: Linear Differential Equations of Order 1
slides.storyContext: Not all real-world problems decay purely exponentially. Sometimes there's an external input—like Arjun's sister getting a new dose of medicine while the old one is still leaving her body.

points.label: Standard form
points.text: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x), where P and Q are functions of x.

points.label: Integrating factor
points.text: Multiply both sides by e^(∫P(x) dx). Left side becomes d/dx[e^(∫P dx) · y].

points.label: Solution
points.text: y = e^(-∫P dx) · ∫Q · e^(∫P dx) dx + C · e^(-∫P dx)

example.problem: Suppose sister takes 250 mg at noon, then 100 mg more at 6 PM, and body eliminates 10% per hour. Model as dy/dx + 0.1y = (input), where input is 0 until 6 PM, then becomes a new dose. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 6: dy/dt + 0.1y = 0. Solution: y = 250 e^(-0.1t). At t = 6, y(6) = 250 e^(-0.6) ≈ 136 mg. Then at t = 6, add 100 mg: new initial condition y(6) = 236 mg. For t > 6: solve anew with y(6) = 236.
example.solution: y(t) = 250 e^(-0.1t) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6, then y(t) ≈ 236 e^(-0.1(t-6)) for t > 6. Concentrations accumulate until body's elimination exceeds intake.

slides.inSimpleWords: If a quantity both decays and receives new input, use linear DE methods to track the balance.

slides.title: Practice: Linear DE
slides.storyContext: Arjun models a simple reservoir that's being filled and drained.

example.problem: Water tank: dV/dt + 0.2V = 5 (inflow 5 L/min, outflow 0.2V). Find V(t) with V(0) = 0. Integrating factor: e^(0.2t). Multiply: e^(0.2t) dV/dt + 0.2e^(0.2t)V = 5e^(0.2t). LHS = d/dt[e^(0.2t)V]. Integrate: e^(0.2t)V = 5∫e^(0.2t) dt = 25e^(0.2t) + C. At t=0: 0 = 25 + C, so C = -25. Thus V(t) = 25 - 25e^(-0.2t).
example.solution: V(t) = 25(1 - e^(-0.2t)). Tank fills toward 25 L as t → ∞.

slides.inSimpleWords: Linear first-order DEs with constant input reach a steady state as t increases.

slides.title: Applications in Science and Engineering
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi shows Arjun real examples: Newton's law of cooling, bacterial growth, radioactive decay, electrical circuits, population dynamics. All are differential equations.

points.label: Newton's Law of Cooling
points.text: dT/dt = -k(T - Tₐ), where T is object temp, Tₐ is ambient temp. Solution: T(t) = Tₐ + (T₀ - Tₐ)e^(-kt).

points.label: Logistic Growth (population)
points.text: dP/dt = rP(1 - P/K), where r is growth rate, K is carrying capacity. Realistic because growth slows as population approaches limit.

points.label: RL circuits (electricity)
points.text: L(dI/dt) + RI = V, where L is inductance, R is resistance, V is voltage. Current I reaches steady state V/R.

example.problem: Hot tea at 80°C placed in room at 25°C. Cooling constant k = 0.05 min⁻¹. What's temperature after 10 minutes? T(10) = 25 + (80 - 25)e^(-0.05×10) = 25 + 55e^(-0.5) ≈ 25 + 55 × 0.606 ≈ 25 + 33.3 ≈ 58.3°C.
example.solution: After 10 minutes, tea is about 58°C—still too hot to drink, but cooling steadily toward room temperature.

slides.inSimpleWords: Differential equations model how real quantities change: temperature, population, current, concentration.

slides.title: Newton's Discovery
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns that Isaac Newton used cooling equations to solve a murder mystery—by calculating when a body died based on its temperature. 'That's CSI, but with calculus!' he laughs.

slides.title: Practice: Newton's Law of Cooling
slides.storyContext: Arjun models a cooling coffee cup.

example.problem: Coffee at 95°C is left in a 20°C room. After 5 minutes, it's 60°C. Find the cooling constant k, then estimate temperature at t = 15 min. Using T(t) = 20 + 75e^(-kt): 60 = 20 + 75e^(-5k) → 40 = 75e^(-5k) → e^(-5k) = 8/15 → -5k = ln(8/15) ≈ -0.62 → k ≈ 0.124 min⁻¹. At t = 15: T(15) = 20 + 75e^(-0.124×15) ≈ 20 + 75e^(-1.86) ≈ 20 + 75×0.156 ≈ 31.7°C.
example.solution: The coffee reaches about 32°C after 15 minutes—cool enough to drink!

slides.inSimpleWords: Use initial conditions to find the cooling constant, then predict temperature at any future time.

slides.title: Homogeneous and Non-homogeneous Equations
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi distinguishes two types of linear equations: those with only y (homogeneous) and those with an extra term (non-homogeneous, like our medicine dose model).

points.label: Homogeneous
points.text: dy/dx + P(x)y = 0. Solution always has the form y = Ce^(-∫P dx).

points.label: Non-homogeneous
points.text: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x), where Q(x) ≠ 0. General solution = (homogeneous solution) + (particular solution).

points.label: Finding particular solution
points.text: Use variation of parameters or method of undetermined coefficients depending on form of Q.

example.problem: Solve dy/dx - 2y = e^(3x). Step 1: Homogeneous part. dy/dx - 2y = 0 has solution yₕ = Ce^(2x). Step 2: Particular solution. Try yₚ = Ae^(3x). Then dyₚ/dx = 3Ae^(3x). Substitute: 3Ae^(3x) - 2Ae^(3x) = e^(3x), so Ae^(3x) = e^(3x), thus A = 1. Step 3: General solution: y = Ce^(2x) + e^(3x).
example.solution: y = Ce^(2x) + e^(3x). With initial condition y(0) = 0: 0 = C + 1, so C = -1, giving y = e^(3x) - e^(2x).

slides.inSimpleWords: Equations with external inputs (like medicine doses) are non-homogeneous. Solve by combining two parts: natural decay and forced response.

slides.title: Full Problem: Antibiotic Therapy
slides.storyContext: Arjun calculates a complete antibiotic model. Dose is 200 mg every 12 hours. Body eliminates 15% per hour. What's the concentration just before the 4th dose (after 36 hours)?

example.problem: Between doses, dM/dt = -0.15M. At each dose, M increases by 200 mg. Solve piecewise: After 1st dose (t=0): M₀ = 200. At t=12⁻ (just before 2nd dose): M = 200e^(-0.15×12) = 200e^(-1.8) ≈ 200 × 0.165 ≈ 33 mg. After 2nd dose: M = 33 + 200 = 233. At t=24⁻: M = 233e^(-1.8) ≈ 38.5 mg. After 3rd dose: M = 38.5 + 200 = 238.5. At t=36⁻ (before 4th dose): M = 238.5e^(-1.8) ≈ 39.4 mg.
example.solution: Just before the 4th dose, concentration is about 39.4 mg. After the 4th dose, it's 239.4 mg. The concentration stabilizes near this level after a few doses.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real therapies involve repeated dosing and exponential elimination—use DEs to predict safe levels.

slides.title: Test Yourself: Water Tank Drainage
slides.storyContext: A cylindrical tank holds water. A tap at the bottom drains it. The rate of drainage is proportional to the square root of the height of water: dh/dt = -k√h, where k = 0.1, h is height in meters.

points.text: If h(0) = 1 meter, find h(t).
How long until the tank is empty (h = 0)?

example.problem: Separate: dh/√h = -0.1 dt. Integrate: 2√h = -0.1t + C. At t = 0, h = 1: 2√1 = C, so C = 2. Thus 2√h = -0.1t + 2, so √h = 1 - 0.05t, hence h = (1 - 0.05t)². Tank empty when 1 - 0.05t = 0, i.e., t = 20 seconds.
example.solution: h(t) = (1 - 0.05t)² for 0 ≤ t ≤ 20. Tank empties in 20 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Separable equations model realistic draining and filling processes in engineering.

slides.title: Exponential and Logistic Growth Models
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi introduces population dynamics: pure exponential growth vs realistic logistic model.

points.label: Exponential growth
points.text: dP/dt = rP gives P(t) = P₀ e^(rt). Population grows without bound.

points.label: Logistic growth
points.text: dP/dt = rP(1 - P/K) with carrying capacity K. Population grows but levels off.

points.label: Logistic solution
points.text: P(t) = K / (1 + ((K - P₀)/P₀)e^(-rt)). Population approaches K asymptotically.

example.problem: Bacterial culture: initial population P₀ = 100, growth rate r = 0.2 per hour. Pure exponential: P(t) = 100e^(0.2t). At t=10: P(10) = 100e^2 ≈ 739. With carrying capacity K = 10,000: P(t) = 10,000 / (1 + 99e^(-0.2t)). At t=10: P(10) ≈ 1,200 (much lower due to resource limits).
example.solution: Logistic model is more realistic for long-term predictions. Population stabilizes near K = 10,000.

slides.inSimpleWords: Logistic equations model real populations that face resource limits. Growth slows as population approaches carrying capacity.

slides.title: Arjun's Realization
slides.storyContext: Arjun finishes solving the tank problem and looks up at his teacher. 'So differential equations are everywhere—medicine, cooling, draining water, populations...' Lakshmi nods. 'Welcome to the language of the universe.'

slides.title: Second-Order Linear Differential Equations
slides.storyContext: Some systems require second-order DEs. Springs, pendulums, and circuits often follow: d²y/dx² + p(dy/dx) + qy = r(x).

points.label: Spring-mass system
points.text: m(d²x/dt²) + b(dx/dt) + kx = 0, where m=mass, b=damping, k=spring constant.

points.label: Characteristic equation
points.text: Assume y = e^(rx). Substitute to get mr² + br + k = 0, which gives exponential or oscillatory solutions.

example.problem: Simple harmonic oscillator: d²x/dt² + 4x = 0. Characteristic eqn: r² + 4 = 0 → r = ±2i. General solution: x(t) = C₁cos(2t) + C₂sin(2t).
example.solution: x(t) = C₁cos(2t) + C₂sin(2t). This oscillates indefinitely at frequency 2 rad/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Second-order DEs often model systems with mass, springs, or damping. Solutions can oscillate or decay exponentially.

slides.title: Beyond the Pharmacist's Shop
slides.storyContext: Arjun's teacher mentions: 'Differential equations govern everything—from drug metabolism to planetary orbits.' Arjun's eyes widen.

slides.title: Practice: Radioactive Decay
slides.storyContext: Arjun applies exponential decay to nuclear decay.

example.problem: Radium-226 half-life: 1600 years. Find decay constant k. At t=1600, M = M₀/2. M(t) = M₀e^(-kt). So e^(-1600k) = 1/2 → -1600k = ln(1/2) ≈ -0.693 → k ≈ 0.000433 yr⁻¹. After 3200 years (2 half-lives): M = M₀e^(-3200×0.000433) ≈ M₀/4.
example.solution: After 3200 years, about 25% of the original remains.

slides.inSimpleWords: Half-life is directly related to the decay constant. Each half-life reduces the amount by 50%.

slides.title: Full Problem: Disease Spread (SIR Model)
slides.storyContext: An epidemic model with three populations: Susceptible (S), Infected (I), Recovered (R).

example.problem: SIR model: dS/dt = -βSI, dI/dt = βSI - γI, dR/dt = γI, where β = transmission rate, γ = recovery rate. For β=0.001, γ=0.1, S(0)=1000, I(0)=10, R(0)=0: At early times, I grows. After I peaks, it declines as recovered individuals are removed. Equilibrium: I → 0, R → (initial S₀ - final S). This models how epidemics burn out.
example.solution: The epidemic peaks when dI/dt = 0, then declines. The final count of recovered depends on transmission rate β and recovery rate γ.

slides.inSimpleWords: SIR models predict epidemic dynamics. Low transmission or high recovery rates minimize total infections.

slides.title: Boundary Value Problems
slides.storyContext: Not all DEs have initial conditions. Sometimes we know values at two endpoints.

example.problem: Heat distribution in a rod: d²T/dx² = 0 with T(0)=100°C (hot end) and T(10)=0°C (cold end). General solution: T(x) = C₁x + C₂. Boundary conditions: T(0)=100 → C₂=100. T(10)=0 → 10C₁ + 100 = 0 → C₁ = -10. So T(x) = 100 - 10x.
example.solution: T(x) = 100 - 10x. Temperature decreases linearly from hot to cold end.

slides.inSimpleWords: Boundary value problems specify conditions at two points instead of initial conditions. Use them to solve for constants.

slides.title: Systems of Differential Equations
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi mentions coupled systems: 'When multiple quantities interact, you need multiple DEs working together.'

slides.title: Systems of First-Order DEs
slides.storyContext: Predator-prey dynamics, multiple chemical reactions, coupled spring-mass systems—all require systems of DEs.

points.label: Lotka-Volterra (predator-prey)
points.text: dx/dt = ax - bxy (prey), dy/dt = -cy + dxy (predators), where x = prey, y = predators.

points.label: Solution behavior
points.text: Populations oscillate cyclically. Prey rises, predators follow, prey crashes, predators starve, repeat.

example.problem: Simple predator-prey: dx/dt = 2x - xy, dy/dt = -y + xy with x(0)=2, y(0)=1. Phase portrait shows closed cycles. Prey peak when predators are low; predators peak after prey peak.
example.solution: System exhibits periodic cycles with lags between predator and prey populations.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coupled DE systems model interactions between populations. Solutions often show oscillations or spirals.

slides.title: Practice: Simple Coupled System
slides.storyContext: Arjun models a simple two-tank mixing problem.

example.problem: Tank 1 contains salt at concentration c₁(t), tank 2 at c₂(t). Flow from 1 to 2: f L/min. dc₁/dt = -f c₁/V₁, dc₂/dt = f c₁/V₁ - f c₂/V₂. With equal volumes V₁=V₂=V and f=1: dc₁/dt = -c₁/V, dc₂/dt = (c₁ - c₂)/V.
example.solution: Tank 1 concentration decays exponentially; tank 2 grows then decays as salt flows through.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coupled systems track multiple interacting quantities. Set up one DE per quantity.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: A differential equation relates a function and its rate of change.
Order is the highest derivative; solution satisfies the equation.
Separable DEs: rearrange to get all y terms on one side, x on the other, then integrate.
Exponential decay/growth: M(t) = M₀ e^(kt) is the solution to dM/dt = kM.
Linear first-order DEs use integrating factor method.
Newton's Law of Cooling, logistic growth, and circuit equations are all differential equations.
Second-order DEs model springs, oscillations, and damped systems.
Real applications: medicine concentration, cooling, population, circuits, draining tanks, epidemics, heat, oscillations.
General solution has arbitrary constants; initial or boundary conditions give particular solutions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Differential equations predict how real systems change over time—essential for medicine, physics, engineering, biology.
